title: Commission of Ezekiel
overview: Ezekiel Chapter 2 marks the beginning of the prophet's divine commission to speak God's message to the rebellious nation of Israel. The chapter captures Ezekiel's encounter with God's spirit empowering him to stand and listen, followed by a solemn charge to confront a stubborn people who have persistently rebelled against God. Despite their resistance, Ezekiel is commanded to deliver God's words faithfully, symbolized by the eating of a scroll containing lamentations and woes. This chapter sets the tone for Ezekiel's prophetic ministry, emphasizing obedience, courage, and the heavy responsibility of proclaiming God's judgment and call to repentance amidst rebellion. It highlights the prophet's role as God's messenger to a nation hardened against divine correction.
structure:
**Verses 1-2: The Prophet’s Empowerment.** Ezekiel is commanded to stand on his feet and receives the Spirit, symbolizing divine empowerment to hear and respond to God's call.

**Verses 3-5: The Mission to a Rebellious People.** God sends Ezekiel to the children of Israel, described as a rebellious nation and house, emphasizing their persistent disobedience and the inevitability that they will recognize a prophet among them.

**Verses 6-7: Encouragement Against Fear.** Ezekiel is instructed not to fear the people's hostility, despite their harshness likened to briers, thorns, and scorpions, underscoring the prophet’s courage and steadfastness.

**Verses 8-10: The Scroll and the Prophetic Word.** Ezekiel is told to listen and not be rebellious like the people; he is commanded to eat a scroll filled with lamentations, mourning, and woe, symbolizing the internalization of God's message he must proclaim.

keyVerses.text: And he said unto me, Son of man, I send thee to the children of Israel, to a rebellious nation that hath rebelled against me: they and their fathers have transgressed against me, even unto this very day.
keyVerses.significance: This verse establishes Ezekiel’s divine commission and highlights the persistent rebellion of Israel, setting the stage for the prophet’s challenging mission to call a disobedient people to repentance.

keyVerses.text: And thou, son of man, be not afraid of them, neither be afraid of their words, though briers and thorns be with thee, and thou dost dwell among scorpions: be not afraid of their words, nor be dismayed at their looks, though they be a rebellious house.
keyVerses.significance: This verse encourages Ezekiel to remain fearless and steadfast despite the hostility and danger posed by the rebellious people, illustrating the courage required for prophetic ministry.

keyVerses.text: But thou, son of man, hear what I say unto thee; Be not thou rebellious like that rebellious house: open thy mouth, and eat that I give thee.
keyVerses.significance: Here God commands Ezekiel to internalize His word by eating the scroll, symbolizing full acceptance and readiness to proclaim God’s message faithfully, contrasting the prophet’s obedience with Israel’s rebellion.

keyVerses.text: And he spread it before me; and it was written within and without: and there was written therein lamentations, and mourning, and woe.
keyVerses.significance: This verse reveals the content of the scroll Ezekiel must consume, emphasizing the sorrowful and judgmental nature of his prophetic message, which reflects the consequences of Israel’s sin.

characters.name: Ezekiel
characters.description: The prophet called by God to deliver His message to Israel. He is empowered by the Spirit to stand firm and speak boldly to a rebellious nation, embodying obedience and courage.

characters.name: God (The LORD)
characters.description: The sovereign sender of Ezekiel, who commissions the prophet to confront Israel’s rebellion. God provides strength, instruction, and the prophetic message symbolized by the scroll.

themes.description: Ezekiel’s calling underscores the theme of God appointing and empowering His servants to proclaim His word, even when the message is difficult and the audience resistant.
The chapter highlights Israel’s persistent rebellion against God, setting the foundation for the prophetic warnings of judgment and the need for repentance.
Ezekiel’s obedience in receiving and internalizing God’s word contrasts with Israel’s disobedience, emphasizing the prophet’s role as a faithful messenger.
The call to not fear opposition or rejection illustrates the courage required to faithfully proclaim God’s truth in hostile environments.

historicalContext: Ezekiel prophesied during the early 6th century BC, a time when the southern kingdom of Judah was under threat from Babylonian conquest, leading to the exile of many Israelites. The nation was spiritually rebellious, having turned away from God through idolatry and disobedience. Ezekiel, a priest and prophet, was among the exiles in Babylon, where he received visions and messages from God to warn and call Israel to repentance despite their stubbornness. The political context was marked by Babylonian dominance and the collapse of Israel’s national identity, making Ezekiel’s prophetic role crucial for preserving hope and divine truth among the exiles.

theologicalInterpretations.description: This perspective emphasizes God’s sovereign calling and the prophet’s obedience as a model for believers. Ezekiel’s commission illustrates the necessity of proclaiming God’s holiness and judgment to a sinful people, trusting God to accomplish His purposes despite human resistance.

Dispensationalists see Ezekiel’s commission as part of God’s unfolding plan for Israel, highlighting the distinction between Israel and the Church. The rebellious nation represents Israel’s hardness, and the scroll’s lamentations foreshadow coming judgments and the eventual restoration of Israel.

Early church interpreters often viewed Ezekiel’s eating of the scroll as a type of Christ’s incarnation and the believer’s reception of God’s word. The prophet’s courage and obedience serve as an example for the faithful to endure opposition while proclaiming divine truth.

crossReferences.connection: Like Ezekiel, Jeremiah is commanded not to fear the people’s words and to stand firm as a prophet to a rebellious nation.
Isaiah receives a commission to speak to a people who will not listen, paralleling Ezekiel’s mission to a stubborn Israel.
John’s eating of the little scroll echoes Ezekiel’s experience, symbolizing internalizing God’s message before proclaiming it.
Paul’s exhortation to Timothy to be bold and not fearful aligns with God’s encouragement to Ezekiel to stand firm despite opposition.
The psalmist’s commitment to internalize God’s word resonates with Ezekiel’s eating of the scroll as a symbol of receiving and treasuring God’s message.

application: Trust God’s Spirit to empower you in difficult tasks and ministry challenges.
Stand firm in obedience to God’s calling, even when facing opposition or rejection.
Internalize Scripture deeply to faithfully proclaim God’s truth to others.
Do not fear the hostility of those who reject God’s message; rely on His strength.
Recognize the seriousness of rebellion against God and respond with repentance.
Commit to speaking God’s word faithfully, regardless of others’ responses.
conclusion: Ezekiel Chapter 2 powerfully introduces the prophet’s divine commission to confront a rebellious Israel with God’s message of judgment and lamentation. It highlights the necessity of courage, obedience, and the internalization of God’s word for faithful ministry. For believers today, this chapter serves as a reminder that God calls His servants to stand firm in truth, empowered by His Spirit, even when faced with resistance. The enduring significance lies in trusting God’s sovereign plan and faithfully proclaiming His word, confident that He will accomplish His purposes despite human rebellion.
timeline: c. 593 BC - Ezekiel’s Commission during the Babylonian Exile

definitions.definition: A title used by God to address Ezekiel, emphasizing his humanity and role as a representative of mankind.
A phrase describing Israel’s persistent disobedience and refusal to submit to God’s authority.
A prophetic symbol meaning to internalize and fully accept God’s message before proclaiming it.
Metaphors for the difficulties and hostility Ezekiel will face from the people he is sent to.
Terms describing the sorrowful and judgmental content of the prophetic message Ezekiel must deliver.
